questions.stem: Which set of characteristics most often makes an environment challenging for permanent human occupation?
options: extreme temperatures, little water, thin air at altitude and isolation
mild temperatures, reliable rainfall, fertile soils and good transport
flat coastal plains with large rivers, ports and natural harbours
a long growing season with frequent, gentle rain and rich volcanic soils
questions.explanation: Environments such as hot and cold deserts, high mountains and polar regions limit food, water and shelter and make supply difficult. Mild, well-watered and accessible places are the ones that attract dense settlement.

questions.stem: In geography, the resilience of a community refers to its:
options: complete independence from outside help, trade and supply networks
ability to cope with, adapt to and recover from challenges and shocks
total population, because larger places always recover more quickly
distance from the nearest capital city and other major service centres
questions.explanation: Resilience is about capacity: how well people absorb a shock, adapt and bounce back. Many resilient communities rely heavily on outside links, so independence is not what defines them.

questions.stem: Many residents of the outback opal-mining town of Coober Pedy in South Australia live in 'dugouts' cut into hillsides. This shows human ingenuity mainly because:
options: the dugouts were built to protect residents from frequent earthquakes
building below ground was required by law to protect the opal deposits
the surrounding rock keeps a steady temperature of about 23 to 25 °C all year
underground homes collect rainwater, so the town needs no other kind of water supply
questions.explanation: Rock and soil insulate dugouts from summer heat that can exceed 40 °C and from cold desert nights, so they stay at a fairly steady comfortable temperature. This low-energy adaptation is a response to the climate, not to earthquakes or law.

questions.stem: Opal was found at Coober Pedy in 1915 and the town grew around mining despite the harsh desert climate. This best illustrates that harsh environments are often occupied because they:
options: are always closer to major cities than more favourable environments
require no infrastructure, so settling there costs much less than elsewhere
offer valuable resources or opportunities that outweigh the difficulties
have climates that become milder once a town has been established there
questions.explanation: Characteristics such as minerals, strategic location or scientific value can make a challenging environment worth occupying. The climate did not change; people adapted to it.

questions.stem: Australia runs year-round research stations at Casey, Davis and Mawson in Antarctica. How does human occupation of these stations differ from that of a desert town?
options: people live there permanently and raise families who attend local schools
the stations are occupied only by tourists during the summer months
there is no permanent population, and staff rotate and rely on outside resupply
the stations are fully self-sufficient, growing all their own food and fuel on site
questions.explanation: Antarctic stations are staffed by expeditioners who serve for a season or a year and depend on ships and aircraft for food, fuel and equipment. No permanent civilian population lives there.

questions.stem: The Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty (1991) is an example of a response that enhances environmental sustainability because it:
options: requires all research stations to close permanently after twenty years
bans mining and requires many kinds of waste to be removed from Antarctica
allows each station to mine the minerals it needs for its own buildings
divides Antarctica into national territories that each country may develop
questions.explanation: The Madrid Protocol designates Antarctica a natural reserve devoted to peace and science, prohibits mineral resource activity other than scientific research and requires wastes such as fuel, plastics and batteries to be taken away. It does not divide the continent between countries.

questions.stem: When a remote mining town's main mine closes, residents turn their unusual homes, landscape and history into a tourism industry. This response best illustrates:
options: dependence on a single industry, which raises vulnerability
resilience through economic diversification after change
abandonment of the environment because occupation failed
a decline in human ingenuity as old industries disappear
questions.explanation: Diversifying the economy helps a community absorb the loss of its main industry and keep its population. Relying on a single industry is the vulnerability that diversification reduces.

questions.stem: A student argues that technology is making challenging environments easy to occupy. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: Technology has removed every single barrier, so all environments are now equally easy to occupy
Technology makes no difference, because harsh environments can never be occupied at all
Technology only matters in cold places, because hot environments are not challenging
Technology lowers some barriers but can increase reliance on outside energy and supplies
questions.explanation: Air conditioning, desalination and modern transport make occupation possible, but they depend on fuel, power and supply chains that can fail. Occupation of harsh places can therefore be more comfortable yet more vulnerable to disruption.

questions.stem: Global economic integration is best defined as:
options: a decline in international trade as countries try to produce everything they need at home
the spread of one shared currency across every country in the world economy
the growing interconnection of economies through trade, investment and flows of people and ideas
the joining of neighbouring countries into a single nation-state with one national government
questions.explanation: Global economic integration links places through flows of goods, capital, labour, information and ideas, often organised by TNCs. Countries remain separate states; their economies become more interdependent.

questions.stem: Which place is best described as relatively unaffected by global economic change?
options: a coastal city built around a special economic zone
a major container port that handles goods for export
a city technology park that runs call centres for global TNCs
a remote village that mainly practises subsistence farming
questions.explanation: Places with little trade, investment or migration, such as remote subsistence communities, are relatively unaffected by global flows. Even such places are rarely completely isolated today.

questions.stem: China made Shenzhen one of its first special economic zones in 1980. Why was Shenzhen's location especially suitable?
options: it bordered Hong Kong, giving access to capital, expertise and a global port
it was China's largest city, so a big workforce was already living there
it lay in the far interior, safely away from foreign economic influence
it had huge coal reserves that powered heavy industry for export markets
questions.explanation: Shenzhen was a small, largely rural area next to Hong Kong, which supplied investment, management skills and shipping links. Its growth came from the zone, not from an existing large population.

questions.stem: Shenzhen grew from a largely rural area in 1980 to more than 17 million people in the 2020 census. Which change to its physical characteristics accompanied this growth?
options: large areas of new forest were planted as farmers left for factory work in the city
the city's rivers became cleaner as industry replaced farming as the main activity
the area of wetland grew as urban drainage systems raised the local water table
farmland, hills and coastline were converted to built-up land and reclaimed sites
questions.explanation: Rapid urban and industrial growth replaced farmland and hills with buildings and infrastructure, and land was reclaimed from the sea. Rivers were heavily polluted during the boom rather than cleaned.

questions.stem: As wages in Shenzhen rose, many low-cost assembly plants moved inland or to South-East Asia, while firms such as Huawei and Tencent grew in the city. This change is best described as:
options: deindustrialisation that has left the city with no remaining industry at all
a return to the farming economy that existed before the zone opened
disinvestment that has caused the city's population to fall sharply
economic restructuring towards high-technology and service activities
questions.explanation: Shenzhen responded to rising costs by moving up the value chain into technology, research and services, while labour-intensive work shifted to cheaper places. The city kept growing, so this is restructuring, not decline.

questions.stem: Toyota and Holden closed their last car factories in Australia in 2017, as car production became concentrated in lower-cost places overseas. Which impact on local places is most likely?
options: a decline in the population of Australia's largest capital cities
job losses in manufacturing suburbs and a shift to service employment
a rapid rise in local manufacturing jobs as factories expanded for export
an increase in car prices because imported cars became illegal
questions.explanation: Global economic integration made it cheaper to import cars than to build them in Australia, so manufacturing districts lost jobs and suppliers. Workers moved into other industries, particularly services.

questions.stem: Global demand for timber, minerals and farmland can bring logging, mining and plantations onto Indigenous Peoples' lands. Which impact is most commonly reported?
options: a guaranteed share of all profits for every community affected
an increase in the area of land under Indigenous control
complete protection of traditional languages and cultures
loss of access to traditional lands, food sources and cultural sites
questions.explanation: Global economic change has often displaced Indigenous Peoples or degraded the land and water they depend on, threatening livelihoods and culture. Responses include land rights claims and the principle of free, prior and informed consent.

questions.stem: In 2017 Shenzhen became the first city to run an all-electric public bus fleet of about 16 000 buses, supported by government subsidies. This is best classified as an opportunity to:
options: reduce the city's population by making public transport much less convenient
slow economic integration by cutting the city's links with foreign markets
enhance environmental sustainability and wellbeing by reducing urban air pollution
increase the city's dependence on imported oil for its public transport system
questions.explanation: Replacing diesel buses with electric ones cuts exhaust emissions in the street, improving air quality and health. It reduces, rather than increases, dependence on imported oil.

questions.stem: In geography, cultural diffusion is:
options: the spread of cultural traits such as language, food or music from place to place
the loss of a culture's traditions because its population has become much older
the division of a country into separate regions with different governments
the movement of people from rural areas to cities in search of better work
questions.explanation: Diffusion describes how ideas, practices and products spread across space, through migration, trade, media or contact. Rural-urban migration can carry culture with it, but it is a population movement, not diffusion itself.

questions.stem: Vietnamese migrants who settled in western Sydney opened restaurants, temples and grocery stores. The spread of Vietnamese culture in this way is an example of:
options: stimulus diffusion, in which only the idea is copied
relocation diffusion, carried by people who moved
hierarchical diffusion, spreading down from leaders
contagious diffusion, spreading by nearby contact
questions.explanation: Relocation diffusion occurs when people migrate and take their culture with them to a new place. In expansion diffusion, by contrast, a trait spreads outwards while staying strong at its source.

questions.stem: McDonald's restaurants in India do not serve beef and offer vegetarian burgers developed for local tastes. This is best described as cultural:
options: adaptation, as a global product is changed to suit local culture
continuity, as the local culture remains completely unchanged
homogenisation, as all places become culturally identical
isolation, as global brands are kept out of the local market
questions.explanation: Adaptation (sometimes called glocalisation) occurs when an introduced trait is modified to fit local beliefs and tastes, here Hindu respect for cows and widespread vegetarianism. The menu change shows the global brand adjusting to India, not making places identical.

questions.stem: Young people in many countries listen to Korean pop music and adopt its fashions. Taking up a cultural trait from elsewhere in this way is called cultural:
options: adoption
continuity
isolation
segregation
questions.explanation: Adoption is when people in a place take up a trait that originated elsewhere. If they then modify it to suit local tastes, that is adaptation.

questions.stem: The rapid spread of the 'Korean Wave' of music, television and film around the world since the 2000s has been facilitated mainly by:
options: colonisation of other countries by Korea in the 20th century
the internet, video streaming and social media platforms
large-scale migration of Korean families to every country
trade agreements requiring other countries to show Korean film
questions.explanation: Digital media are powerful mediums of cultural change because they let content reach global audiences instantly and cheaply. Migration and trade also carry culture, but they cannot explain such fast, worldwide spread.

questions.stem: France's Toubon Law of 1994 requires the use of French in areas such as advertising, product instructions and workplace documents. This is best described as a response that aims to:
options: speed up the adoption of English as the official national language of France
encourage the diffusion of French culture by banning foreign travel
promote cultural homogenisation across all European Union countries
protect the continuity of a national culture against outside influence
questions.explanation: The law responds to concern about the spread of English by protecting the French language in public life. It is a form of cultural protection, not a ban on travel or a move towards a single European culture.

questions.stem: Restaurants in a multicultural city serve dishes that blend Korean and Mexican cooking. Which concept best describes this outcome of cultural change?
options: homogenisation, as one culture replaces all the others in the city
continuity, as each culture's traditions are kept separate and unchanged
segregation, as different cultural groups are kept apart in separate areas
hybridisation, as traits from different cultures combine into something new
questions.explanation: Hybridisation produces new forms by mixing elements of different cultures. Homogenisation is the opposite outcome, in which places become more alike as local differences disappear.

questions.stem: In an inner-city suburb, new cafes and apartments replace older shops. Long-term residents say the suburb's character is being lost, while newcomers welcome the changes. This shows that responses to cultural change:
options: are decided only by governments, so residents' views do not matter at all
depend on people's perceptions, which vary with their connection to the place
are the same for everyone, because all residents experience change equally
are always negative, because any change to a place damages its culture
questions.explanation: Different groups perceive the same change differently, depending on their attachment to the place, interests and values. Geographers investigate these varying perceptions rather than assuming a single response.

questions.stem: A nation-state is best defined as:
options: a sovereign state whose people largely share a common national identity
any group of people who share a language but have no government of their own
a region within a country that has its own parliament and laws
a group of countries that cooperate for defence and trade purposes
questions.explanation: A state is a sovereign political unit with territory and government; a nation is a people with a shared identity. A nation-state combines the two, although few states are culturally uniform.

questions.stem: The Kurds, numbering tens of millions, live mainly across parts of Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria but have no independent state. Geographically, they are best described as:
options: a power bloc, because they cooperate across several countries
an external territory governed by a single neighbouring state
a nation without a state, spread across several state borders
a nation-state, because they share a common language and culture
questions.explanation: The Kurds share a strong national identity but no sovereign state of their own, and their homeland is divided by international borders. This mismatch between nation and state has long been a source of political tension.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a power bloc?
options: NATO, a military alliance of North American and European states
the Kurds, a people living across several Middle Eastern states
Antarctica, a continent reserved for peace and scientific research
Shenzhen, a city that grew rapidly in a special economic zone
questions.explanation: A power bloc is a group of states that align to pursue shared political, military or economic interests, such as NATO, the European Union or ASEAN. Blocs shape the geopolitical characteristics of places from a global perspective.

questions.stem: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal state's exclusive economic zone extends up to:
options: 200 nautical miles from its baselines
12 nautical miles from its baselines
24 nautical miles from its baselines
350 kilometres from its national capital
questions.explanation: Within an exclusive economic zone a state has rights over fishing, oil, gas and other resources. The 12-nautical-mile limit is the territorial sea, where the state has full sovereignty.

questions.stem: Parts of the South China Sea are claimed by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei. Which combination of factors best explains why the area is so contested?
options: rich fisheries, possible oil and gas reserves and vital shipping routes
fertile farmland on the islands and large permanent island populations
a shortage of fresh water on the mainland that the islands could easily supply
a shared cultural heritage that each country wants to protect alone
questions.explanation: Economic factors (fish, energy and trade routes) and strategic military value make control of the sea and its small islands valuable. Most of the features are tiny reefs and rocks with no farmland or large populations.

questions.stem: In 2016 an arbitral tribunal under the Law of the Sea Convention found that China had no legal basis for historic rights within its 'nine-dash line'. China rejected the ruling. This most clearly shows that:
options: international law has limited power to resolve disputes without enforcement
the ruling ended the dispute, since all claimants then accepted the decision
the tribunal awarded the whole South China Sea to the Philippines
the Law of the Sea Convention does not apply to any disputes at sea
questions.explanation: The tribunal, in a case brought by the Philippines, ruled against China's broad claim, but there is no body able to enforce the decision, and tension continued. The ruling concerned maritime rights and did not award sovereignty over the whole sea.

questions.stem: In the South China Sea, reefs have been dredged and built up into artificial islands with runways and ports. Which environmental impact of this political tension is most direct?
options: an increase in fish stocks because the new islands provide extra shelter
a fall in sea level around the islands as sand is moved onto the reefs
improved water quality as the new runways filter runoff from the land
destruction of coral reef habitat and smothering of nearby reefs by sediment
questions.explanation: Dredging and reclamation bury living coral and stir up sediment that damages surrounding reefs, on top of pressure from competing fishing fleets. The impacts reduce, rather than increase, marine habitat.

questions.stem: Some researchers propose that the claimants in a contested sea set aside sovereignty and jointly manage fisheries and marine protected areas. This is best classified as an opportunity to:
options: increase the catch by removing all limits on fishing in the disputed area
end political tension by closing the shipping routes through the area
enhance sustainability by cooperating on shared resources despite the dispute
resolve the dispute by awarding all of the sea to the most powerful state
questions.explanation: Joint management can protect fish stocks and reefs without anyone having to give up their sovereignty claim, so it can work even when the dispute itself is unresolved. Removing limits on fishing would speed the decline of stocks.

questions.stem: In a network, the places that are connected (such as cities, ports or airports) are called:
options: nodes
links
flows
corridors
questions.explanation: Networks are made of nodes joined by links (routes such as cables, roads or flight paths), along which flows of people, goods or data move. Highly connected nodes are called hubs.

questions.stem: How is most intercontinental internet data carried between continents?
options: through radio towers placed on islands at sea
through fibre-optic cables laid on the sea floor
through satellites in orbit high above the Equator
through high-voltage power lines between countries
questions.explanation: Undersea fibre-optic cables carry the great majority of international data because they have far greater capacity and lower delay than satellites. Satellites serve mainly remote places and act as backup.

questions.stem: The first transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in 1858, and the first transatlantic fibre-optic cable (TAT-8) entered service in 1988. The key technological advance of fibre optics was:
options: sending data as pulses of light, carrying vastly more information
sending signals by radio waves, so no cable was needed on the sea floor
using copper wires for the first time, making cables much cheaper
carrying electricity as well as messages, powering coastal towns
questions.explanation: Fibre-optic cables carry data as light through glass fibres, giving enormous capacity and speed compared with earlier copper cables. This advance underpins the modern global internet.

questions.stem: A map of undersea internet cables shows dense routes across the North Atlantic and North Pacific but far fewer to many African countries and Pacific islands. This spatial pattern of the network mainly reflects:
options: the depth of the ocean, since cables cannot be laid across the deep Atlantic
laws that ban cable landings in countries with smaller populations
the location of volcanoes, which cables must pass close to for power
the concentration of demand and investment in wealthy, connected regions
questions.explanation: Cable companies invest where demand and revenue are greatest, so wealthy regions are densely linked while poorer or remote places have fewer routes. The Atlantic is deep, yet it has some of the densest cable routes in the world.

questions.stem: In January 2022 the eruption of the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcano cut Tonga's only international undersea cable, and the country had very limited internet for about five weeks. What does this most clearly show?
options: satellite links had already fully replaced undersea cables in Pacific countries
networks make places less connected, so Tonga gained from the outage
places with a single link are vulnerable, so backup routes add resilience
undersea cables cannot be repaired once they have been damaged at all
questions.explanation: With no second cable, one break isolated Tonga, disrupting communication, banking and business; only limited satellite links remained until a ship repaired the cable. Redundant routes are a common response to this vulnerability.

questions.stem: From the 1960s, London's inner docks declined as container ships moved to larger, deeper ports downstream, and the area was later redeveloped as offices and housing at Canary Wharf. This best shows how changes in a network can:
options: only affect rural places far from major cities
transform places by shifting activity between nodes
leave places unchanged, as ports never change location
reduce trade, because container ships carry less cargo
questions.explanation: Containerisation, a technological advance in the shipping network, needed deep water and large terminals, so port activity moved away from the old docks. The abandoned docklands were then transformed by new land uses.

questions.stem: Airlines based in Dubai and Singapore route many long-distance passengers through their home airports to connect with onward flights. This network structure is called:
options: hub-and-spoke
point-to-point
linear corridor
dispersed grid
questions.explanation: In a hub-and-spoke network, flights from many places feed into a central hub where passengers change planes. This has turned hub cities into major nodes of global movement, with jobs in aviation, tourism and logistics.

questions.stem: Data centres that run cloud services and streaming use large amounts of electricity and, often, water for cooling. Which response best enhances environmental sustainability while keeping the network operating?
options: moving all data centres to deserts, where water for cooling is most plentiful
using more diesel generators so that data centres need less mains electricity
powering data centres with renewable energy and using more efficient cooling
banning all data centres so that internet services stop operating entirely
questions.explanation: Renewable power cuts the greenhouse gas emissions linked to data centres, and efficient cooling reduces water and energy use. Deserts are short of water, and diesel generation would raise emissions.
